Part 1 of 7

Industry and Big Business Grow

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 1: Explain the primary factors that stimulated unprecedented industrial and agricultural growth in the late nineteenth century.

Core Objective 2: Describe the entrepreneurs who pioneered the growth of Big Business, the goals they aimed to achieve, and the strategies they used to dominate their industries.

Core Objective 3: Evaluate the role of the federal government in the nation’s economic development during this period.

IN MY WORDS: In your own words, what helped American industry grow so fast after the Civil War?

Reading AThe Second Industrial Revolution

The dramatic increases in economic productivity after the Civil War were driven by the Second Industrial Revolution, which began in the mid-nineteenth century.

Centered in the United States and Germany, the Second Industrial Revolution resulted from three related developments. The first was the creation of modern transportation and communication systems that gave farmers and factory owners access to national and international markets. The completion of transcontinental railroads and the development of oceangoing steamships helped expand markets worldwide . . . During the 1880s, a second breakthrough—the harnessing of electrical power—accelerated the pace of change in industrial and urban development. . . . The third major catalyst for the Second Industrial Revolution was the systematic application of scientific research to industrial production.

Word help: productivity = how much gets made · markets = places to sell goods · harnessing = putting to use · catalyst = something that speeds up change · systematic = careful and organized

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 16, “The Elements of Industrial and Agricultural Growth” (The Second Industrial Revolution) (p. 687).

Reading BRockefeller, Carnegie, and Big Business

In 1870, Rockefeller teamed with his brother William and two other businessmen to establish the Standard Oil Company of Ohio. . . . Early on, he pursued a strategy called horizontal integration, in which a dominant corporation buys or forces out most of its competitors.

By 1879, Standard Oil controlled more than 90 percent of the nation’s oil refining business. The company had become a monopoly, a business so large that it controls an entire industry. . . . Standard Oil eventually owned everything it needed to produce, refine, and deliver oil. . . . In economic terms, this business strategy is called vertical integration.

In 1882, Rockefeller tried to hide his efforts to gain a monopoly by organizing the Standard Oil Trust. A trust gives a corporation (the “trustee”) the legal power to manage other companies at the same time.

Like Rockefeller in the oil industry, Carnegie came to dominate the steel industry, acquiring competitors or driving them out of business by cutting prices and taking their customers.

Word help: competitors = rival companies · dominant = most powerful · refining = cleaning crude oil into products · acquiring = buying · phase = step

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 16, “The Rise of Big Business” (John D. Rockefeller; Andrew Carnegie) (p. 698).

Reading CGovernment and Business

Equally important in propelling the post–Civil War economic boom was what federal, state, and local governments did not do. During this laissez-faire period, there were no sweeping investigations of business practices, no legislation to protect workers and consumers, and no effective regulatory laws or commissions.

The supportive relationship between business and political leaders played a significant role in economic development during the decades after the Civil War. The willingness of Congress to impose high tariffs on imported goods, allocate government-owned lands to railroad companies and settlers in the West, and exercise only limited oversight of business dealings were crucial factors in promoting industrial expansion.

Word help: laissez-faire = “leave it alone”; government stays out of business · regulatory = making rules for business · tariffs = taxes on goods from other countries · allocate = give out · oversight = watching over

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 16, “The Alliance of Business and Politics” (Laissez-faire) (p. 703).

The government’s role. Use Reading C. Name two things the federal government DID to help business grow, and one thing it did NOT do.

A Changed Society and Workers Organize

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 4: Analyze the ways in which the nation’s class structure and the lives of women changed in the late nineteenth century.

Core Objective 5: Describe how wage earners organized unions to promote their interests during this period.

IN MY WORDS: Why would workers want to join a union instead of working alone?

Reading DA New Middle Class and New Roles for Women

In addition to an increasing number of millionaires, the Gilded Age witnessed the rise of a middle class. . . . Most middle-class Americans working outside the home were salaried employees of large businesses who would later be called “white-collar” professionals: editors, engineers, accountants, supervisors, managers, marketers, and realtors. Others, mostly unmarried women, were clerks, secretaries, salespeople, teachers, nurses, and librarians.

The growing presence of middle-class women in the workforce partly reflected the increasing number of women enrolled in colleges. Dozens of women’s colleges were founded after the Civil War, and many formerly all-male colleges began admitting women. By 1900, a third of college students were women.

Word help: Gilded Age = the late 1800s, a time of great wealth for a few · salaried = paid a set amount each year · white-collar = office work · enrolled = signed up

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 16, “A Changed Social Order” (A Growing Middle Class; Middle-Class Women) (p. 705).

Reading EWorking Women and Children

Employers often recruited women and children for the unskilled jobs because they were willing to work for lower wages than men. Many women, especially young immigrants, worked in sweatshops where they endured long hours; low pay; and cramped, dimly lit, unventilated working conditions. . . . In the manufacturing sector, women’s wages averaged $7 a week, compared to $10 for unskilled men.

Child labor increased as parents desperate for more income put their children to work. By 1880, one of every six children under age fourteen was working full-time; by 1900, the United States had almost 2 million child laborers.

Word help: recruited = hired · unskilled = not needing special training · sweatshops = crowded, hot workshops · unventilated = with no fresh air · desperate = in great need

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 16, “A Changed Social Order” (Working Women; Child Labor) (p. 707).

Reading FThe Knights of Labor

In 1869, another national labor group emerged: the Noble Order of the Knights of Labor. . . . Under Powderly’s leadership, the Knights of Labor offered membership to all workers except lawyers, doctors, bankers, those who sold liquor—and the Chinese. By recruiting more types of workers, the Knights became the nation’s largest labor union. In the early 1880s, their number soared from about 100,000 to more than 700,000.

Powderly promoted cooperation and mutual understanding between labor and management. He believed that labor disputes should be resolved through peaceful negotiation and arbitration rather than strikes or violence.

Word help: labor = workers · labor union = a group of workers who join together · management = the bosses · arbitration = letting an outside person settle a fight

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 16, “Organized Labor” (The Knights of Labor).

Reading GHaymarket and the AFL

What came to be called the Haymarket Riot grew indirectly out of prolonged agitation for the eight-hour workday. . . . At that point, someone threw a bomb into the ranks of blue uniforms that left dozens maimed or killed. The police then fired into the fleeing crowd, resulting in more casualties.

Thus, in 1886, delegates from twenty-five craft unions organized the American Federation of Labor (AFL). . . . Unlike Terence Powderly and the Knights of Labor, Gompers focused on concrete economic gains—higher wages, shorter hours, and better working conditions.

Word help: agitation = protest · ranks of blue uniforms = the police lines · casualties = people hurt or killed · craft unions = unions of skilled workers · concrete = real and specific

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 16, “Organized Labor” (The Haymarket Riot (1886); Samuel Gompers and the AFL).

Reading HHomestead and Pullman

Andrew Carnegie, who had previously expressed sympathy for unions, now wanted to destroy the union so that he would no longer have to negotiate with workers over wages and working conditions. . . . Carnegie and Frick, with the support of local, state, and national officials, had eliminated the union.

During the depression of 1893, George Pullman laid off 3,000 of his 5,800 employees and slashed wages by 25 to 40 percent for the rest . . . Finally, on July 3, President Grover Cleveland sent thousands of federal troops to the Chicago area, claiming it was his duty to ensure delivery of the mail on the trains.

Word help: negotiate = talk to reach a deal · eliminated = got rid of · slashed = cut deeply · federal troops = U.S. Army soldiers

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 16, “Organized Labor” (The Homestead Steel Strike; The Pullman Strike (1894)).

Source 1Two Views of the Homestead Steel Strike, 1892 (Primary Sources)

The first quote is from Terence Powderly, leader of the Knights of Labor, in a magazine in September 1892. The second quote is from the Philadelphia Times, a newspaper, after the strike ended in November 1892.

“Those who harshly criticise the workmen of Homestead should put themselves in the place of these workmen. . . . Then step outside of the mill and witness the erection of a high fence and its armament. . . . by the light of the blazing guns at Homestead, it was written that arbitration must take the place of “Pinkertonism.”
“The Homestead strike was simply a monument of folly when all the surrounding circumstances are considered. . . . It was the weak against the strong . . . The surrender of the strike is a confession that any employer that has the courage and the means to make the battle can overthrow it”

Word help: criticise = say bad things about · erection = building · armament = weapons · arbitration = letting an outside person settle a fight · Pinkertonism = using hired armed guards against workers · folly = foolish act · overthrow = defeat

Terence V. Powderly, “A Knight of Labor’s View of the Homestead Strike,” The North American Review, September 1892; “The Lesson of Homestead,” Philadelphia Times, November 22, 1892. In Norton, Ch. 16, “Organized Labor,” Comparing Perspectives: “The Homestead Steel Strike, 1892” (pp. 718–719).

Source 1. (1) What did Powderly say should replace “Pinkertonism”? (2) What did the Philadelphia Times call the strike?

The “New South” and Sharecropping

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 6: Describe the vision for the “New South” after the Civil War.

Core Objective 7: Describe what the sharecropping system in the postwar South entailed and how it constricted the lives of poor farmers.

IN MY WORDS: What did leaders of the “New South” want the South to become?

Reading IThe Lost Cause and the New South

Novelists, poets, and former Confederate leaders fashioned what came to be called the Lost Cause legend—a sanitized version of the region’s history in which the romanticized Confederacy had done no wrong . . . Nostalgic apologists for the Confederacy glamorized the old plantation culture and insisted that secession and the Civil War had little to do with slavery

A few prominent southerners, however, rejected the Lost Cause version of the Civil War. These politicians, editors, and business leaders called for a New South to replace the pre–Civil War Old South. They wanted to displace the dominant planter elite and diversify the region’s agricultural economy by developing a growing industrial sector.

Word help: legend = a story that is not fully true · sanitized = cleaned up to hide the bad parts · glamorized = made to look better than it was · planter elite = rich plantation owners · diversify = add new kinds · industrial sector = factories and industry

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “The Legend of the Lost Cause” (A Vision of a New South) (p. 728).

Reading JMills and Cigarettes

The chief accomplishment of the New South movement was a dramatic expansion of the textile industry, which produced cotton thread, bedding, and clothing. From 1880 to 1900, the number of cotton mills in the South grew from 161 to 400 . . . Seventy percent of millworkers were younger than twenty-one, and many were under fourteen.

In 1890, he forced his four largest competitors to join him in creating the American Tobacco Company, which controlled nine-tenths of the nation’s cigarette production. The new enterprise enabled Duke to dominate the tobacco industry.

Word help: textile = cloth · expansion = growth · he = James “Buck” Duke, a North Carolina tobacco businessman · enterprise = business

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “The Legend of the Lost Cause” (Developing a Textile Industry; The Tobacco Industry).

Reading KSharecropping

Many rural areas adopted a barter economy in which a “crossroads” merchant would provide food, clothing, seed, fertilizer, and other items to poor farmers “on credit” in exchange for a share of their crops (a system called “sharecropping”). Blacks and Whites who had nothing to offer a farm owner but their labor worked the owner’s land in return for shelter in a small cabin. In exchange, they had to “share” a portion of their crop with the landowner

Many of the African American “sharecroppers” worked for the same planter who had owned them before the Civil War. “The colored folks,” said a Black Alabama sharecropper, “stayed with the old boss man and farmed and worked on the plantations. They were still slaves, but they were free slaves.”

Word help: barter = trading goods instead of using money · merchant = store owner · on credit = take now, pay later · portion = part

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “The Failings of the “New South”” (Sharecropping) (p. 732).

MapMap 17.1: Sharecropping, 1880–1900

This modern textbook map shades each state by how many of its farmers were sharecroppers or tenants in 1900. Dots show how fast that number grew from 1880 to 1900.

Map key: Darkest green = over 55 percent of all farmers · Lighter colors = fewer sharecroppers · Big black dot = grew over 10 percent from 1880 to 1900 · Open circle = went down

Norton, Ch. 17, Map 17.1, “Sharecropping, 1880–1900.” Modern textbook map.

Part 4 of 7

Jim Crow in the South

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 8: Explain how and why White southerners adopted “Jim Crow” segregation laws and stripped most African Americans of their voting rights by the end of the nineteenth century.

IN MY WORDS: In your own words, what were “Jim Crow” laws?

Reading LTaking Away the Vote

Mississippi took the lead in stripping Blacks of voting rights. The so-called Mississippi Plan (1890), a series of amendments to the state constitution, set the pattern of disenfranchisement that most southern states would soon follow.

Third, to vote, people had to have paid all taxes on time, including a so-called “poll tax”—a restriction that hurt both poor Blacks and poor Whites. Finally, the new state constitution required that all voters had to be able to read or at least “understand” the U.S. Constitution. White registrars, however, decided who satisfied this requirement, and they frequently discriminated against Blacks.

Word help: amendments = changes · disenfranchisement = taking away the right to vote · poll tax = a fee to vote · registrars = officials who sign up voters · discriminated = treated unfairly

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “The Origins of Jim Crow Segregation” (Disenfranchising African Americans).

Reading M“Separate but Equal”

In the Plessy case in 1896, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that states could create laws segregating public places such as schools, hotels, and restaurants. . . . The Plessy ruling endorsed racially “separate but equal” facilities in virtually every area of southern life—schools, parks, theaters, rail and trolley cars, saloons.

The new regulations requiring racial segregation came to be called Jim Crow laws. . . . Signs reading “Whites Only” or “Colored Only” above restrooms and water fountains emerged as hallmarks of the Jim Crow system of racial segregation.

Word help: Plessy = Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), a Supreme Court case · segregating = separating by race · endorsed = approved · facilities = places and buildings · hallmarks = clear signs

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “The Origins of Jim Crow Segregation” (Plessy v. Ferguson (1896); Jim Crow Segregation).

Reading NWilmington, 1898

In 1894 and 1896, Wilmington’s Black voters, a majority in the city, had elected African Americans and White Republicans to various city offices. . . . Whites rampaged through the polling places, forcing Blacks out at gunpoint and stuffing ballot boxes to ensure that White candidates won. . . . they killed sixty, wounded dozens, and destroyed homes and businesses. . . . As a result of the Wilmington insurrection, more than 2,000 African Americans fled the state or were forced out at gunpoint.

Word help: Wilmington = a city in North Carolina · rampaged = rushed around violently · polling places = where people vote · insurrection = violent uprising against a government

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “The Origins of Jim Crow Segregation” (The Wilmington Insurrection (1898)) (p. 737).

Reading OTwo Black Leaders Respond

In a famous speech at the Cotton States and International Exposition in Atlanta in 1895, Booker T. Washington urged the African American community not to migrate to northern states or to other nations but to “cast down your [water] bucket where you are . . . African Americans first needed to become self-sufficient economically. Civil rights would have to wait.

Du Bois called Washington’s 1895 speech the Atlanta Compromise and said that he would not “surrender the leadership of this race to cowards”

Word help: urged = strongly asked · migrate = move · self-sufficient = able to take care of yourself · compromise = giving up part of what you want · Du Bois = W.E.B. Du Bois, a Black scholar and activist

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “The Origins of Jim Crow Segregation” (Booker T. Washington; W.E.B. Du Bois) (p. 743).

Settling the New West

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 9: Identify the various groups of migrants to the West after the Civil War, and the reasons they migrated.

Core Objective 10: Describe the diverse experiences of miners, farmers, ranchers, cowboys, women, and Mexican Americans in the West in the late nineteenth century.

IN MY WORDS: Give two reasons people moved West after the Civil War.

Reading PWho Went West?

During the second half of the nineteenth century, migrants flowed into what had been the largely Indigenous and Hispanic West. . . . The largest number of Western immigrants came from northern Europe and Canada. . . . More than 200,000 Chinese arrived in California between 1876 and 1890, joining some 70,000 others who had come earlier to build railroads and work in mining communities.

After the collapse of federal reconstruction efforts in the postwar South, thousands of African Americans migrated westward. Some 6,000 arrived in Kansas in 1879, and as many as 20,000 followed the next year. They were called Exodusters because they were making their exodus from the region of southern White supremacy in search of a haven from racism and poverty.

Word help: migrants = people who move to a new place · exodus = leaving a place in large numbers · haven = safe place

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “The Settling of the New West” (The Migratory Stream; The African American Migration) (p. 746).

Reading QCowboys, Miners, Farmers, and Women

Cowboys were mostly unmarried young men—the average age was twenty-four—willing to work seven days a week, often in bad weather. More than a third of them were Hispanic American, African American, or Native American.

Along the South Platte River, not far from Pikes Peak in Colorado, a prospecting party found gold in 1858, and the glistening news brought perhaps 100,000 “fifty-niners” into the area by the next year. . . . Farming amid the unforgiving environment and harsh weather of the Great Plains was brutal. . . . Few, however, actually did get rich.

In 1869, Wyoming became the first territory to grant women the right to vote (suffrage).

Word help: prospecting party = group searching for gold · fifty-niners = gold seekers who came in 1859 · Great Plains = the flat grasslands in the middle of the country · territories = western lands that were not yet states · suffrage = the right to vote

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “Life in the New West” (Cowboys; Gold and Silver; Farming on the Plains; Women’s Voting Rights).

Reading RMexican Americans in the Southwest

Mexican Americans found themselves outnumbered, outvoted, and—eventually—outcast. Sheriffs and judges discriminated against Mexican Americans in land disputes; railroads, mines, and ranchers paid Mexican Americans less than Anglo-Americans . . . Spanish-speaking children were expected to attend “Mexican schools” separate from White children.

Mexican American citizens at times rebelled against the efforts of Whites to seize their lands. In 1889, in New Mexico, three Herrera brothers—Juan Jose, Pablo, and Nicanor—organized Las Gorras Blancas (The White Caps) to evict White “land grabbers”

Word help: outcast = pushed out of society · discriminated = treated unfairly · land disputes = fights over who owns land · evict = force out

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “Life in the New West” (The Hispanic Southwest; Las Gorras Blancas (White Caps)) (p. 759).

Indigenous Peoples and the End of the Frontier

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 11: Evaluate the impact of the federal government’s post-Civil War policies in the West on the Indigenous peoples who had long lived in the region.

Core Objective 12: Describe how the South and West had changed by 1900.

IN MY WORDS: In one sentence, how did government policies in the West affect Indigenous peoples?

Reading SSand Creek

Despite that promise, at dawn on November 29, 1864, Colonel John M. Chivington’s 700 militiamen attacked a camp of Cheyenne and Arapaho along Sand Creek, about forty miles from Fort Lyon. . . . As the horse soldiers approached, Black Kettle, the Cheyenne chief, waved first an American flag and then a white flag, but the soldiers paid no heed. Over seven hours, they slaughtered, scalped, and mutilated 165 peaceful Native Americans—men, women, children, and the elderly. Back in Denver, Chivington was greeted as a hero.

Word help: that promise = Colorado’s governor had promised these Cheyenne and Arapaho protection at Fort Lyon · militiamen = citizen soldiers · paid no heed = did not pay attention · slaughtered = killed many people cruelly

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “The Fate of Western Indigenous Peoples” (The Sand Creek Massacre) (p. 762).

Reading TThe Ghost Dance and Wounded Knee

Late in 1888, Wovoka (or Jack Wilson), a Paiute in western Nevada, fell ill. In a delirium, he imagined being in the spirit world, where he learned of a deliverer coming to rescue the Indigenous peoples and restore their lands. . . . The Ghost Dance movement spread rapidly.

On December 29, 1890, a bloodbath occurred at an Indigenous camp in South Dakota, along a frozen creek called Wounded Knee. . . . More than 150 unarmed Native American men, women, and children died in the Battle of Wounded Knee

Word help: delirium = a confused state from sickness · deliverer = someone who saves people · restore = give back · bloodbath = mass killing

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “The Fate of Western Indigenous Peoples” (The Ghost Dance) (p. 768).

Reading UThe Dawes Act

Well-intentioned but misguided White reformers sought to “Americanize” Indigenous people by promoting passage of the Dawes Severalty Act of 1887 (also called the General Allotment Act), the most sweeping policy directed at Native Americans in U.S. history. . . . it divided tribal lands and “allotted” them to individuals, granting 160 acres to each head of a family and lesser amounts to others.

A Kiowa chief named White Bear said that his nomadic people did “not want to settle down in houses. . . . I love to roam over the wild prairie. There I am free and happy.” But his preferences were ignored. Between 1887 and 1934, Native Americans lost an estimated 86 million acres of ancestral lands.

Word help: misguided = wrong-headed · “Americanize” = make them live like White Americans · allotted = handed out in parts · nomadic = moving from place to place · ancestral = handed down from their ancestors

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “The Fate of Western Indigenous Peoples” (A Century of Dishonor) (p. 769).

Reading VThe South and West by 1900

The 1890 national census data indicated that the frontier era was over; Americans had spread across the entire continent in large numbers.

By 1900, the South and West were quite different from what they had been in 1865. In the West, mechanized commercial agriculture changed the dynamics of farming, and large-scale hydraulic mining replaced panning for gold. By the end of the nineteenth century, many homesteaders had been forced to abandon their farms and become wage-earning laborers . . . As discontent rose among farmers and farmworkers in the South and the West, many joined the People’s Party, whose followers were known as Populists

Word help: census = the official count of people · frontier = the edge of settled land · mechanized = done by machines · homesteaders = settlers given land to farm · discontent = anger and unhappiness

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 17, “The End of the Frontier” (Discontented Farmers) (p. 770).

Part 7 of 7

CER: Opportunity or Hardship?

BIG QUESTION

Did the changes of 1865–1900 bring more opportunity or more hardship to ordinary Americans?
